Revision note (v2.8): The violation catalog is consolidated into a single Master Violation Catalog
covering three scenarios in one place — Full Integrity Mode, Browser Integrity Mode (Candidate),
and Browser Integrity Mode (Learner) — replacing the earlier separate Section A/B/F/G split. “Light
Integrity Mode” is renamed “Browser Integrity Mode” throughout. Learner runs in Browser Integrity
Mode only — there is no Learner + Full Integrity Mode combination, since app installation is not
available on managed Cognizant laptops through the standard route. The Learner column is
deliberately thinner, with several violations marked NA where they would create false positives in a
corporate/office environment (shared corporate VPN, dual monitors as standard equipment,
colleagues in the background, IT remote-support tools). Two violations (Tab Switch/Focus Loss,
Fullscreen Exit, and Prohibited Object Detected) use an occurrence threshold for Learner — the
first one or two occurrences are not scored, only repeated occurrences count — to avoid penalizing
routine workplace interruptions. All weight and Trigger Count values in the new catalog are
proposed defaults, not sourced from prior documentation, pending Platform Admin and evaluation
team confirmation.
Purpose: This document captures only MUST-HAVE technical capabilities and system behaviors
required to support the AI-first BRD and user stories. Decision logic, policy mechanics, escalation
rules, and audit evidence details are intentionally excluded to keep this document concise and
implementation-focused.

1.1 Question Bank – Human Review Triggers (Risk Indicators)
• High decision-impact flag: item is part of a high-stakes or heavily weighted assessment stage.
• Data dependency risk: missing or unstable datasets, schema mismatches, or forbidden
external dependencies.
• Framework dependency risk (project items): build failures, dependency/version drift, or
starter-code defects.
• Runtime / resource anomaly: excessive time/memory usage or sandbox policy violations.
• Duplicate / near-duplicate detection: high similarity with existing or previously retired items.
• Answer key / rubric inconsistency: incorrect expected outputs, broken reference solutions, or
missing rubric evidence.
• Content safety / compliance risk: biased language, accessibility gaps, or policy non-
compliance.
• Candidate challenge / dispute: repeated candidate flags, appeals, or negative feedback
beyond threshold.
• Integrity correlation: abnormal correlation with plagiarism, similarity spikes, or integrity
violations.
• Exposure / leakage risk: exposure thresholds breached, repeated reuse across drives, or
external leakage signals.
• Weak discrimination: flat score distribution indicating poor differentiation across proficiency
levels.
• Difficulty confidence mismatch: predicted difficulty materially deviates from observed
candidate performance.
• Solution instability: flaky or inconsistent test results across repeated executions.
• Non-determinism risk: multiple valid outputs without clear acceptance criteria or
environment-dependent outcomes.
• Ambiguity risk: unclear problem statements, missing constraints/examples, or multiple
plausible interpretations.
Human review shall be triggered when one or more of the following indicators are detected
(thresholds are policy-configurable). Note: this Question Bank human-review mechanism is
unrelated to assessment integrity review — no integrity-related attempt requires manual review
anywhere in this platform (see Section C).
The Question Bank lifecycle is AI-led by default. Human (SME / Governance) review is invoked only
when specific risk indicators are detected, ensuring scale, consistency, and audit defensibility
without routine manual intervention.
2. Integrity Violation Catalog, Weightages, and Integrity Index Logic
Purpose: This section is the single technical reference for integrity violation definitions, default
weightages, and the Integrity Index computation logic. User stories must reference this section
instead of duplicating rule definitions. There is exactly one integrity score — the Integrity Index. No
separate IRS, Credibility Index, or Severity scale exists anywhere in this platform.
A. Master Violation Catalog — All Scenarios
This single catalog covers three scenarios in three columns: Full Integrity Mode (secure app,
Candidate only), Browser Integrity Mode — Candidate (standard browser, external hiring
candidates), and Browser Integrity Mode — Learner (standard browser, internal associates on
managed Cognizant laptops). “NA” means the violation does not apply in that scenario — either
because it cannot be technically detected there, or because it was deliberately excluded to avoid
false positives in that context.

B. Detection Notes
• Coding-behaviour signals (paste burst, typing speed, pause-then-burst, correction ratio, first-
compile-success, clipboard-without-shortcut, time-to-first-character, IDE-shortcuts) require
the Runtime Engine to capture and stream keystroke telemetry in real time — event type,
millisecond timestamp, character delta, cumulative code block length. Raw keystrokes are
never stored, only aggregated metrics.
• Network signals (VPN, TOR, shared IP, RDP-latency, disconnects) are captured server-side by
the Runtime Engine — IP reputation lookups and cross-attempt IP comparison require no
client-side software.
• Webcam-based signals (face match, additional person, multiple faces, face not visible,
prohibited object) are captured via standard browser webcam access in both Full and
Browser Integrity Mode — no native application is required for webcam capture itself.
• The occurrence-threshold pattern (Prohibited Object, Fullscreen Exit, Tab Switch for Learner)
means the platform counts occurrences per attempt but does not log a scored violation event
until the threshold is crossed — this is a deliberate false-positive guard for a corporate/office
environment, not a detection limitation.
C. Integrity Index — Computation Logic (Combined Model)
The Integrity Index is the platform's single integrity score. It combines a weighted score across
Standard Violations with a fixed override from Zero-Tolerance Violations. There is no separate IRS,
Credibility Index, or Severity scale — all are superseded by this one model. Computation happens
once, after submission, in five steps:
• Step 0 — Select the active catalog column from Section A, based on both the persona
attempting the assessment and the assessment's configured Integrity Mode: (Learner,
Browser Integrity Mode) uses the Learner column; (Candidate, Browser Integrity Mode) uses
the Browser Mode — Candidate column; (Candidate, Full Integrity Mode) uses the Full
Integrity Mode column. There is no (Learner, Full Integrity Mode) combination.
• Step 1 — Classify every violation that fired as Standard or Zero-Tolerance, per the selected
column.
• Step 2 — Raw violation score: sum of (weight × count) across Standard violations only, from
the selected column. Zero-Tolerance violations do not contribute to this sum. This raw score
is uncapped — it can exceed 100 if violations recur enough times (e.g., a single violation firing
many times can alone push the raw score well past 100).
• Step 3 — Normalize the score: derive a normalized score by capping the raw score at 100. If
raw score ≤ 100, normalized score = raw score, unchanged. If raw score > 100, normalized
score = 100, flat. The raw score and the normalized score are both persisted against the
attempt record — the raw score preserves how far past the threshold an attempt actually
went, for report detail and reviewer context; the normalized score is what all banding,
dashboards, and downstream consumers use, since it is always a clean 0–100 value.
• Step 4 — Band the normalized score using the tier boundaries configured by Platform
Admin (default: 0–29 / 30–59 / 60–100) and convert to a trust tier in reverse: Normalized Low
band → High trust. Normalized Medium band → Medium trust. Normalized High band → Low
trust. This is the score-based result.
• Step 5 — Zero-Tolerance override: if any Zero-Tolerance violation fired at or beyond its
Trigger Count (from the selected column), the Integrity Index is forced to Low trust, regardless
of the Step 4 result. This override always wins.
• The Integrity Index is always expressed with the word “trust” attached (High trust / Medium
trust / Low trust), never as a bare Low/Medium/High.
• No attempt is held, queued, or flagged for human review at any step, under any
circumstance. This model is entirely automatic.

C.1 Plain-Language Violation Detail
A plain-language detail is generated and stored against the attempt record only when the final
Integrity Index is Low trust. All other attempts store the fixed text “No significant violations noted.”
This detail carries no reviewer guidance and recommends no action — it is descriptive only, for
report display.
• If Low trust was reached by Zero-Tolerance override: the detail names the specific Zero-
Tolerance violation(s) that fired and their count.
• If Low trust was reached by score alone: the detail names the top contributing Standard
violations by weight.
• Example (override): “Developer tools were opened once during the attempt. Developer tools
access is treated as a Zero-Tolerance violation regardless of frequency.”
• Example (score-based): “Multiple faces were detected on 4 occasions, and the candidate
exited fullscreen mode 3 times. Together these contributed to a high overall violation score.”
C.2 Data Persistence
For every completed attempt, the following is persisted to the attempt record during proctoring
evaluation:
• Which catalog column was used (persona + Integrity Mode combination).
• Raw violation score (Standard violations only, from that column).
• Every violation that fired, with its count and category (Standard / Zero-Tolerance).
• The final Integrity Index tier (High trust / Medium trust / Low trust).
• Whether the final tier was reached via the score band (Step 3) or via Zero-Tolerance override
(Step 4).
• The plain-language violation detail text, or the fixed “No significant violations noted.” text.
• This data is retained per the platform's evidence retention policy and is never modified after
being written — append-only, same as the audit log.
D. Identity Verification — Face Match / Mismatch (AI-based)
The platform shall perform continuous AI-based face match verification to ensure that the person
taking the assessment matches the registered candidate identity. Face match verification
compares a pre-registered candidate photo captured during onboarding or assessment setup
against live webcam frames during the assessment. The system shall use facial landmark vectors,
eye-region features, and passive liveness detection to compute a face-match confidence score. If
the live face does not match the registered photo beyond the configured confidence threshold, a
Face Mismatch violation shall be raised — classified Zero-Tolerance, Trigger ≥ 3, per Section A.1.
Reference implementations: industry-grade facial verification solutions such as HyperVerge Face
Authentication demonstrate that passive face match with standard webcams can achieve
approximately 98–99% accuracy with strong spoof resistance. The platform remains vendor-
agnostic and may use any compliant internal or external engine that meets these accuracy and
liveness requirements.
E. Plagiarism Detection (Coding Questions Only — Hiring Drives, Candidate Only)
Plagiarism is evaluated only for coding-type questions. Every submission for a given coding
question is compared against every other submission for that same question within the same
assessment drive (cohort) — never against submissions from a different drive, and never against
external internet sources. Any starter code or function signature template provided to every
candidate is stripped out before comparison, since identical shared code should never count
toward similarity.
Outcome is one of three values: Not Applicable (detection could not run — fewer than 2
submissions for the question, no submission made, submission empty or failed to compile, or a
technical failure during detection), Acceptable (similarity falls within what is normal for that
specific question's cohort), or Not Acceptable (similarity is a statistical outlier for that question, or
exceeds the absolute configured ceiling).
A flat similarity percentage alone is not sufficient to decide the outcome: an easy, highly-
constrained question naturally produces high similarity across many independent, honest
submissions, so the correct comparison is against that question's own peer group, not a single
fixed number applied identically to every question.
The configured plagiarism threshold (default 90%, range 70–99%) remains configurable via
Platform Admin, but now serves as an absolute backstop ceiling rather than the sole decision
mechanism — a submission can still be flagged Not Acceptable for crossing this ceiling even if it is
not a statistical outlier for its question, and conversely a submission below this ceiling can still be
flagged if it is an extreme outlier relative to its cohort.
Plagiarism outcome is never an input to the Integrity Index — it feeds the Decision Policy
independently, as before.
F. Proficiency Level Naming
Cognizant standard is PL1 (entry level) / PL2 / PL3 — there is no PL0. This is used consistently in
Section J below. The platform's Blueprint taxonomy (referenced in CAD-17 and QB generation
parameters) still uses PL0 Learner / PL1 Practitioner / PL2 Specialist, which predates this
correction and needs the same fix — flagged here as a cross-cutting item for the Content Admin /
QB stories, not resolved within this document.
G. Rubric Configuration for Evaluation — Fixed Weight Model
Weight per dimension is fixed by Platform Admin configuration, per Question Type and Proficiency
Level where an override exists. This weight is identical for every question of that type and level — AI
does not decide or adjust weight distribution at runtime, under any circumstance. AI retains one
and only one degree of freedom: it may select which dimensions are active for a given question
(within the enabled set and the Min–Max count) based on difficulty. Once dimensions are selected,
their weight is read from configuration, not chosen.

J. Rubric Configuration for Evaluation — Fixed Weight Model
Weight per dimension is fixed by Platform Admin configuration, per Question Type and Proficiency Level
where an override exists. This weight is identical for every question of that type and level — AI does not
decide or adjust weight distribution at runtime, under any circumstance. AI retains one and only one degree
of freedom: it may select which dimensions are active for a given question (within the enabled set and the
Min–Max count) based on difficulty. Once dimensions are selected, their weight is read from configuration,
not chosen.

predates this correction and needs the same fix — flagged here as a cross-cutting item for the Content
Admin / QB stories, not resolved within this section.

3. Communication Assessment — Evaluation Rubrics, Sub-dimension
Weightage & Scoring User Stories
3.1 Purpose of This Section
The existing user stories (COM-CND-08 to COM-CND-16) define what the candidate does in each
workspace — play audio, record speech, read a passage, write a response. This section adds, from
the companion documents:
• The evaluation rubric for each section type
• The confirmed sub-dimension weightage for each section.
• Three new Scoring Engine user stories (COM-SCR-03, COM-SCR-04, COM-SCR-05) that
implement sectional domain score computation and CEFR calculation.
3.2 Universal Scoring Formula — All Rubric-Scored Sections
Source: CommAssessment_Rubrics_Weights_ScoringUS_v1.2.docx, Section 2 header note. All
dimension scores are rated 1–5 by the AI engine. The same two-step formula applies to every
rubric-scored section (Listening, Speaking Fluency, Reading, Writing):
Step 1 — Raw Score = sum ( dimension score x weight )
Step 2 — Domain Score (0–100) = ((Raw Score - 1) / 4) x 100
This formula normalises the 1–5 raw rating range to a 0–100 platform score. The formula is
deterministic — the AI engine does not adjust weights or scores at runtime.

Listening Raw Score = (Literal Comprehension x 0.40) + (Inferential Understanding x 0.35) +
(Instruction Following x 0.25)
Listening Domain Score (0-100) = ((Raw Score - 1) / 4) x 100 | Threshold: >= 60 to pass.
Worked example (from source document):
• Literal Comprehension: 4.0 x 0.40 = 1.60
• Inferential Understanding: 3.5 x 0.35 = 1.225
• Instruction Following: 4.0 x 0.25 = 1.00
• Raw = 3.825 -> Domain Score = ((3.825 - 1) / 4) x 100 = 70.6 -> PASS (>= 60) -> CEFR: B2
